claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure with multilevel chemical fluctuations.

Coupling a reduced-order multiscale physics model with physics-informed machine learning and active learning will enable rapid, accurate prediction of Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness.
A reduced-order model can explicitly capture the local chemical fluctuations and microstructural heterogeneity of hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
The multiscale model can extract local stress fields, microstructural heterogeneity, and effective stress-intensity factors as predictive descriptors.
Stress-intensity factors and plastic-flow criteria can be imposed as physics constraints in the machine-learning model.
Active learning can refine this model using targeted low-cost experiments.
Descriptors of local microstructure and chemical fluctuations mediate the connection between elastic, plastic, and fracture behavior and the model predictions.
A reduced-order multiscale model provides interpretable descriptors by capturing important physical interactions across multiple length scales.
Combining physics-derived descriptors and constraints with active learning will iteratively improve predictions.
Active learning will overcome sparse high-fidelity data specifically for fracture toughness.
The combined approach will reduce computational time by more than 50% relative to the stated baseline methods.
The combined approach will improve predictive accuracy for Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness by approximately 15–20%.
Full first-principles calculations are computationally demanding for alloy discovery.
CALPHAD modeling can require significant computational resources.
CALPHAD accuracy for high-entropy alloys can be limited by the absence of reliable databases.
Conventional machine-learning models are insufficient for capturing fracture toughness.
The proposed approach is reliable only while the microstructure remains within the previously characterized hierarchical regime.
New phases or drastic changes in the scale of chemical fluctuations would reduce model reliability.
Insufficient experimental data for active learning would reduce model reliability.
Prior successes combining physical modeling, machine learning, and active learning in high-entropy or refractory alloys support the feasibility of the proposed approach.
